title: Teach me more: hearing it again
hook: the son keeps asking, and the father never sighs
carry: hear it, reflect on it, sit with it
tomorrow: a face from years ago, older now. how is it the same person?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rivers ran from the sea, to the sea, with Paul's one blood beside them: we come from Being, and forget it. Today the whole week comes back, and so does the son's request.

The fifth but why in a row, from a kid in the back seat. It's hard not to sigh. Teach me more, sir, Shvetaketu says, again and again. And his father never says, I already told you. He says: so be it, my dear. Then he finds another picture.
screen: `THE FIFTH 'BUT WHY?'` → `TEACH ME MORE, SIR.` → `SO BE IT, MY DEAR.`

segments.voice: Listen to how the refrain climbs. That which is the finest essence, this whole world has that as its self. That is the real. That is the self. That you are. So that isn't pointing somewhere vague. The father has named it in the same breath: the finest essence, the real, the self. And each time his son asks again, he climbs the same stairs with a new picture. Now the week, in one breath. Vamadeva said I was Manu, and the sun, even now. A father promised the unheard made heard, and held up clay. Being alone wished to be many. A sleeper went home like a bird to its post. Many trees made one honey, and the tiger stayed a tiger. Rivers from east and west came from one sea, and Paul spoke of one blood. Under each picture, the same request: teach me more. And that's a real Hindu teaching about learning. In another Upanishad, the sage Yajnavalkya tells his wife Maitreyi the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on. Vedanta teachers built a path from those words: shravana, hearing the teaching; manana, thinking it through; nididhyasana, sitting with it until it's yours. That's why students hear tat tvam asi again and again. The great teacher Shankara even points to this very chapter: the father says it nine times, he notes, because most of us need to hear it more than once. It's why families tell the Ramayana every Diwali, and the same verses return at every puja. Asking once more isn't failing. It's the method.
screen: `THE FINEST ESSENCE, THE REAL, THE SELF.` · `CLAY, A BIRD, HONEY, RIVERS.` · `HEAR, REFLECT, SIT WITH IT.` · then, large: `ASKING AGAIN IS THE METHOD.`

segments.voice: Try the three steps in small. Say tat tvam asi softly once, and just hear it. Then think of one picture from this week, clay, the bird, the honey or the rivers, and what it shows. Then sit a minute in silence with the words, and when the mind wanders, come back without scolding: so be it, my dear.
Tat tvam asi: that you are, where that is the finest essence, the real, the self. The week's word, still climbing.
For keeps: hear it, reflect on it, sit with it. That's how the great sayings are learned. That's the week.

screen: `DAY 1757 COUNTS.` → `TAT TVAM ASI · 6 OF 9.` → `TOMORROW: OLDER NOW. HOW IS IT THE SAME PERSON?`

howItsDone: In Vedanta study, a great saying is learned by shravana, manana and nididhyasana (hearing, reflecting, meditating), a path teachers draw from Brihadaranyaka 2.4.5; Chandogya 6, where the son keeps asking and the father keeps answering, is read as a model of that patience.

fork.setup: a friend reads 'that you are' and says 'that' is too vague to mean anything. what does the refrain point to?
options: the finest essence, the real, the self, named in the same breath.
a far-off heaven that the text never describes at all.
whatever each reader happens to want it to mean.
fork.reveal: the refrain names it first: the finest essence, the self of this whole world, the real, the self. only then: that you are.

original.note: Sanskrit: anima, the finest essence the refrain names before 'that you are'.

chat.meaning: In the Chandogya the son keeps asking and the father answers 'so be it, my dear' each time; Vedanta teaches a truth is heard, reflected on and meditated on, again and again.

Shvetaketu.meaning: the son who keeps asking: teach me more

Vamadeva.meaning: the seer who said: I was Manu, and the sun

Chandogya.meaning: the Upanishad where tat tvam asi is taught

Yajnavalkya.meaning: a sage of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad

Maitreyi.meaning: Yajnavalkya's wife, who asked him about the self

shravana.meaning: hearing the teaching, the first of three steps

Shankara.meaning: the 8th-century Vedanta teacher who explained why the saying is repeated

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 (that which is the finest essence, this whole world has that as its self; that is the real, that is the self, that you are, Shvetaketu; 'teach me more, sir'; 'so be it, my dear')
Chandogya Upanishad 6.9–6.13 (the bees and honey, the rivers and the sea, the tree, the banyan seed, the salt in water; each closes with the refrain and the son's request)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.10; Chandogya Upanishad 6.1–6.2; Taittiriya Upanishad 2.7.1; Acts 17:26 (the week's look-back)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5 (Yajnavalkya to Maitreyi: the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on; the basis Vedanta teachers give for shravana, manana and nididhyasana)
Brahma Sutra 4.1.1–2 with Shankara's commentary (repetition of the teaching; Shankara cites the repeated tat tvam asi to Shvetaketu)
